summary: Reports on an investigation by the Year 2000 Working Group into how the Year 2000 problem could affect Internet protocols as documented in RFCs. It found little reason for concern with the protocols themselves. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Before the year 2000, people worried clocks would break. A team checked the rule books of the Internet and mostly found they would be fine.

questions: which internet protocols had y2k problems
what is a sliding window for two digit years
subtitle: The IETF's audit of RFCs 1 through 2128 for Year 2000 date bugs, and what it found.

tldr.problem: Trade press suggested that the Internet would collapse at midnight on 31 December 1999, because many programs and some protocols store the year as two digits.
tldr.mechanism: The Year 2000 Working Group scanned the RFCs in groups by protocol area, examined every hit for date or time fields, and reported which protocols have two-digit years or fields that roll over.
tldr.outcome: Almost all protocols got a clean bill of health. A few older ones used two-digit years, and several use a 32-bit signed count of seconds since 1 January 1970 that turns negative in 2038. The report itself expects newer RFCs to make it obsolete.

today: RFC 2626 is an Informational RFC, published in June 1999, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the state of RFCs 1 through 2128 at that time, and its own disclaimer says that newer RFCs superseding the old ones are expected to make its information obsolete.

sections.title: Why the Internet Needed an Audit
sections.content:
The Year 2000 problem (also called the millennium problem) comes from software and some protocols using a two-digit field for the year. The RFC notes that the trade press expected billions of dollars of spending on it, and that the first articles suggested the Internet would collapse at midnight on 31 December 1999.

To counter this and to spare countless companies from repeating the same investigation, the IETF set up the Year 2000 Working Group. It made an inventory of the important Internet protocols documented in the RFC series. Only protocols directly related to the Internet were considered.

The abstract gives the verdict up front: little reason for concern about the protocols' functionality, a few older implementations still using two-digit years (as in RFC 850), and several "period" problems where a time field rolls over when its size is reached.
sections.plainLanguage: People were scared that the Internet would break when the calendar changed to 2000. So a group checked the rulebooks once, so that every company did not have to check them all again.

sections.title: Scope and Disclaimer
sections.content:
The report says plainly that it is not complete. It tried to analyze the Year 2000 impact on hundreds of protocols and is likely to have missed some and misunderstood others. Nobody should claim legitimacy or approval for a protocol based on it, and its proposed solutions are only proposals that need a formal engineering review.

The research covered RFCs 1 through 2128. At that time the IESG was chartered not to allow new RFCs with Year 2000 issues, and some fixes had already followed. For example, RWhois (RFC 1714) was updated, and RFC 2167 documents the fixed version. The report expects newer RFCs to make its information obsolete, and says the group's work is truly complete only when the document is completely obsolete.

Other special dates, such as the first leap year, January 10, 2000 or January 1, 2001, were suggested. The report finds no place where the RFC series' protocols use days in this way, so it sees little reason to expect an impact.
sections.plainLanguage: The team admits it may have missed some things, like a checker who skims a huge pile of homework. It also expects later rulebooks to fix what it found.

sections.title: How the Search Was Done
sections.content:
The group sorted the RFCs into logical groups instead of following publication order. Each group was assigned to a team. Many hundreds of RFCs were eliminated immediately based on content, and RFCs below 400 were considered too obsolete to consider.

At a minimum each team used an automatic scanning system, case-insensitively, for these strings: date, GMT, UTCTime, year, yy (not part of yyyy), two-digit, 2-digit, 2digit, century, 1900 and 2000. Teams could also read each RFC in full and, in some cases, the reference implementation's source code.

A hit is not automatically a bug, since all of those strings except UTCTime can appear alongside a date format that handles the year 2000 correctly. So every hit was examined individually. Cases that cause no problem, such as a year stored as a two-byte integer or a four-character display string, are not discussed in the report. Appendix B of the RFC is the PERL program used for a first cut, and Appendix C is its output.
sections.plainLanguage: The team searched the rulebooks for words like year and date, then looked at every spot it found to see if it was really a problem. Most spots were harmless.

sections.title: Two-Digit Years That Were Found
sections.content:
The real Year 2000 problems were few and mostly in older or niche protocols:

  • HTTP. HTTP 1.1 (RFC 2068) requires newly generated dates in the RFC 1123 format, which is compliant, but still requires acceptance of the older RFC 850 format with a two-digit year. The report notes that many existing servers, serving on the order of one fifth of the current HTTP traffic, sent dates in the ambiguous format. RFC 2068 tells clients and caches to assume an RFC 850 date that appears more than 50 years in the future is really in the past.
  • Mail. RFCs 821 and 822 originally required two-digit years, but RFC 1123 strongly recommended four digits. Two-digit mail dates will not "fail", but might be mis-sorted. IMAP versions 1, 2 and 3 used two-digit years, while IMAP version 4 requires four.
  • Network news. NNTP (RFC 977) requires YYMMDD dates in the NEWGROUPS and NEWNEWS commands, and the Usenet message format (RFC 1036) also specifies a two-digit year. A working group had been formed to update the news protocols.
  • Paging. Versions 2 and 3 of the Simple Network Paging Protocol use a YYMMDDHHMMSS+/-GMT format for the HOLDuntil option, which the report says is clearly invalid after the end of 1999.
  • UTCTime. Several directory, SNMP, security and PEM documents use the ASN.1 UTCTime type, which has a two-digit year. SNMP's MIB definitions use YYMMDDHHMMZ to record module history, so management applications must prepend "19" or "20" as appropriate.

Other minor cases include the RIPE routing registry objects in RFC 1786, which use YYMMDD identifiers, and SIFT/UFT (RFC 1440), which has an optional DATE command of the form mm/dd/yy.

One non-protocol case is DNS zone file serial numbers written as YYXXXXXX. The serial only has to increase (see RFC 1982), so a change from 99 to 00 would be a decrease and is not permitted. Switching to a four-digit year before it next needs updating is always safe.
sections.plainLanguage: A few old rules wrote years as just two numbers, like 99. When the year after 99 comes, a computer might think it went backwards in time. The team listed where that could happen.

sections.title: Rollover Dates Beyond 2000
sections.content:
The report also looked at "period" problems, where a time field fills up and wraps around. The biggest group is the year 2038. Many protocols store the number of seconds since January 1, 1970 in 32 bits, and a signed 32-bit value turns negative at Tue Jan 19 03:14:07 GMT 2038.

Examples include the DNS Security signature time (RFC 2065), the Inter-Domain Policy Routing (IDPR) timestamp, an optional RADIUS time attribute, and the Snoop packet capture file format. The report refers the DNS Security issue to the appropriate working group. It says the IDPR authors recognized the 2038 problem but felt the protocol would not be in use by then.

Other rollovers come later or earlier. The Time Protocol (RFC 868) counts seconds since 1 January 1900 and rolls over at Thu Feb 07 00:54:54 2036 GMT. NTP is described as having no knowledge of the millennium. NFS keeps its times as 32-bit unsigned seconds since 1970-01-01 and does not hit an epoch event until 2106, and RTP's NTP-style 64-bit time format has a period problem in 2106 (RFC 1889).
sections.plainLanguage: A counter with only so many digits fills up, like a car odometer going back to zero. The team listed which Internet counters will fill up and when.

sections.title: Suggested Fixes
sections.content:
The real solution, according to the report, is to use four-digit year fields in applications and hardware. For counters measured from a fixed date, a protocol can define a wrapping solution, define a larger number space than 32 bits, or make more efficient use of the 32-bit space. Because currently deployed systems cannot all be replaced, workarounds for existing data are needed too.

Two interpretation rules are described for two-digit years:

  • Fixed window. A two-digit year YY of 50 or more is read as 19YY, and a value below 50 is read as 20YY. It is simple and easy to deploy, so it might be the most commonly adopted fix, but it only postpones the problem 40 to 50 years until an artificial Year 2050 problem.
  • Sliding window. Pick a value N. Any two-digit year up to the current two-digit year plus N is treated as future, and any other as past. Its advantages are that no new fixed year problems are introduced and that different applications can choose different values of N. The drawback is that it is harder to implement, and N needs to be constant across implementations to work well.

The report stresses that these are proposals only, to be reviewed before adoption.
sections.plainLanguage: One fix is a simple rule: numbers 50 and up mean the 1900s, and smaller ones mean the 2000s. Another fix moves the cutoff along with the calendar, which is smarter but trickier.

sections.title: Results by Protocol Area
sections.content:
The bulk of the document (sections 7 through 22) walks through the protocol groups one by one. Most come out clean:

  • Autoconfiguration (BOOTP, DHCP, IPv6 autoconfiguration): no problems. Times are 32-bit integers in seconds, which allow lease times of well over 100 years.
  • Network and transport layer (IP, TCP, UDP, PPP, ICMP, ARP, RPC): after review of nearly 400 RFCs, no Year 2000 problems were found.
  • Name services (DNS): no protocol problems, apart from the zone serial habit and the 2038 timestamp end of life in DNS security.
  • Routing (RIP, OSPF, BGP, IDRP): RIP and BGP are compliant. BGP has no knowledge of absolute time, only relative time.
  • Virtual terminal (Telnet, TN3270, SSH): found compliant.
  • Disk sharing (NFS): no Year 2000 problems.

The remaining sections cover directory services, games and chat, information services and file transfer, electronic mail, network time, network management, news, real-time services, security and a catch-all "Other" group. For these, the sections give per-RFC notes, and long lists of RFC numbers that were reviewed and found to contain no date or time references, or were not available for review. Appendix A lists every RFC examined, by area.

The Kerberos version 5 specification (RFC 1510) uses a generalized time format with four-digit years. The report adds that the MIT reference implementation by default set ticket expiration to December 31, 1999, which is not a protocol issue but could have operational impact.
sections.plainLanguage: For most groups of rules the team wrote 'all clear'. Where something was off, they wrote a short note saying which rule and what could go wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The report considers the implications of various security protocols, and says no additional security considerations are needed. It acknowledges that a potential Year 2000 problem may cause some security problems, but states that those are problems of specific applications rather than protocol deficiencies introduced in this document.

Within the security protocols themselves, the audit noted that PEM certificates and the DASS protocol use UTC time with two-digit years, which could cause trouble. For PEM certificates, RFC 1422 notes the lack of a century, so comparisons across centuries must be done with care. The report says poorly written software might prematurely expire or validate a certificate, although no current software was known to do so.
sections.plainLanguage: The team says the report itself adds no new safety worries. A confused clock could still cause trouble in a particular program, such as one that wrongly decides a pass has expired.
